title: Long lives, slow births
teaches: Why bats live several times longer than mammals their size, one pup a year and slow recovery, and what bats and viruses really show
summary: **Bats live far longer than their size predicts.** A 7 g Brandt's bat has lived 41 years, where a house mouse, three times heavier, lives two or three.

**Across mammals, bigger animals live longer.** Bats reach on average about three and a half times the lifespan that line predicts for their size, the small hibernating bats ten times, and birds sit high too.
**Flying away from danger may be the reason.** Animals that predators seldom kill gain from bodies built to last; torpor and better repair of DNA are other ideas, still being tested.
**Most bats raise one pup a year.** It is born at a quarter to a third of its mother's weight, from sperm stored over the winter since autumn mating.
**So bat colonies recover slowly.** A colony that loses most of its members takes decades to rebuild, and a small extra death rate every year can outrun its births.
**Inflammation is the body's alarm, and it also does damage.** Bats seem to keep theirs turned down, which may let them carry viruses without falling ill.
**Bats are not unusual virus carriers for their numbers.** They carry about as many viruses that infect people as their number of species predicts, no more per species than other groups.
**Rabies is rare in wild bats but deadly to people.** Under 1% of wild bats carry it; never handle a bat with bare hands.

parts.title: Forty-one years in a Siberian cave

blocks.text: In 2005 bat researchers working in the caves of southern Siberia caught a male Brandt's bat, *Myotis brandtii*, a small brown bat of Europe and Asia that weighs about 7 g, as much as seven paper clips. On its forearm it carried a numbered metal band. The records showed the band had been put on in the same cave region in the 1960s, when the bat was already an adult. It was at least 41 years old, and still flying.[^band] Andrej Podlutsky and his colleagues reported it as the oldest bat known.

A house mouse weighs about three times as much. In a laboratory, with food, warmth and no predators, a mouse lives two or three years; in the wild it rarely sees a second winter. Nearer home, a little brown bat, the commonest bat of the northern United States, has been found alive 34 years after it was banded. Small mammals are supposed to live fast and die young, and these bats do neither. The question for this lesson is why, and what a long, slow life means for a bat population when something like white-nose syndrome strikes.

Across mammals, bigger animals tend to live longer. A shrew lives a year or three, a rabbit up to nine, a horse up to about sixty, an elephant seventy. Plotted on scales where each step is a tenfold change, the longest known lives of ground mammals fall close to a straight line that rises gently with body mass: on it, a mammal a thousand times heavier lives roughly five times as long.

blocks.caption: The longest known life of each animal against its body mass, both on ratio scales. The dashed line is fitted to the ground mammals alone. Lifespans are rounded records, mostly from the AnAge database; many come from animals in zoos.
blocks.task: Guess how long the bat can live

blocks.text: Every bat in the figure has a longest known life above the line. Gerald Wilkinson and Jason South, working through records for 64 species in 2002, found that bats live on average about three and a half times as long as ground mammals of the same size, and the small hibernating bats of the north are the extreme cases, ten times or more. In the whole of the mammals only a handful of others come close: the naked mole-rat, a hairless African rodent that lives its whole life in closed underground burrows, and humans. Birds, the other flyers, sit above the line too.

Animals do not simply wear out like machines; how fast they age is itself shaped by evolution. The usual explanation goes like this. Building a body that lasts costs energy: repairing damaged DNA and proteins, replacing cells, keeping defences up. If an animal is likely to be eaten within a year anyway, as most wild mice are, energy spent on a body that could last thirty years is wasted, and evolution favours putting it into breeding fast instead. If an animal is seldom killed by predators, a body built to last pays, because it will be around to use it.

Flight is a good way not to be eaten. A bat spends its day hidden in a cave or crevice and its night in the air, out of reach of most hunters, so the theory predicts bats should age slowly, and the figure shows they do. Birds, which escape predators the same way, sit above the line too. Steven Austad tested the idea in a different animal: opossums on Sapelo Island, off Georgia, which has been cut off from the mainland for some four thousand years and has none of its foxes or bobcats. The island opossums aged more slowly than mainland ones.[^austad]

Other ideas sit alongside this one. Wilkinson and South found that bats that hibernate live longer than those that do not, and a body that spends months of the year at a few degrees above freezing may simply age less in that time. Studies of the genes of Brandt's bats and other *Myotis*, the mouse-eared bats, suggest they repair damaged DNA unusually well. In some of them the **telomeres**, the protective caps on the ends of each chromosome (the long threads that carry an animal's DNA), do not shorten with age as ours do. These are hypotheses being tested, not settled answers; they may all play a part, and they help explain how bats can live long, while the predator argument explains why it pays them to.

The other side of a long life is a slow start to each new one. Most bats raise a single pup a year. A house mouse can breed at six weeks old and raise a litter of five or six every month through the summer; a female little brown bat breeds once a year, at most, from her first or second summer.

Her timetable is odd. Little brown bats mate in late summer and autumn, at the entrances of the caves where they will hibernate, and through the winter. The female does not ovulate then. She stores the sperm in her womb through months of torpor, and only when she wakes in spring does she release an egg and become pregnant.[^stored] Pregnant females gather in warm maternity colonies, in attics, barns and hollow trees, and give birth in June. The pup is enormous, a quarter to a third of its mother's weight: for a 60 kg woman, a baby of 15 to 20 kg, the weight of a four-year-old. It hangs on to her and drinks her milk for about three weeks, flies by four weeks old, and must lay down its own fat for winter in a few weeks more.

A population like that cannot grow fast. Count only the females: each year about 85 in 100 adults survive. Each of the 100 has one pup, half of them female, and about half of those survive their first year, so 100 mothers add about 25 young females. A colony at best gains 25 and loses 15 for every 100, a net tenth a year. The figure asks what that means after a disaster.

blocks.caption: A model colony of little brown bats, as a share of the most its roost can hold. The sliders set the pups each female has a year, a one-off loss in one bad winter, and extra deaths every year after it. In the model 85% of adult females survive each year, half the young survive their first year, and growth slows as the roost fills. The dashed line is mice after the same loss.
blocks.task: Guess, then raise the extra yearly deaths until the colony cannot make them up

blocks.text: After a 90% loss the model colony takes over forty years to come back, while mice are back within a year. Give the bats two or three pups a year and they recover in a decade or less, which is why the single pup matters. The third slider is the quieter danger: a colony that can add at most a tenth a year, after its normal deaths, is lost if something new kills more than a tenth of its members every year on top of them, whether a fungus, wind turbines (lesson 10 comes back to these) or a sealed-up roost.

Bats have a reputation as carriers of disease, and some dangerous viruses do live in them, among them rabies, and Marburg virus, a relative of Ebola, in Egyptian fruit bats. A **virus** is a packet of genes in a protein coat that can multiply only inside the cells of a host. What puzzles people is that bats often carry such viruses without seeming ill.

To see the ideas, start with **inflammation**. When a body's cells sense damage or an invader, they send out chemical signals that call in immune cells, make blood vessels leak fluid into the tissue, and can raise the body's temperature in a fever. It is the body's alarm, and it fights infection, but it also damages the body's own tissue; much of the harm in a severe infection comes from the alarm rather than from the virus itself.

Two ideas, both hypotheses, try to explain bats. The first, put forward by Thomas O'Shea and colleagues in 2014, is that flight is a nightly fever. A flying bat burns energy many times faster than at rest, and its body temperature can climb above 40 °C, as a fever would push it; viruses that live in bats may have been selected to survive that heat. The second is that bats keep their alarm turned down. Laboratory studies of bat cells have found several of the sensors that start inflammation, which detect signs of an invader such as stray DNA inside a cell, working more weakly than in other mammals, so a bat may live with a virus, letting it multiply at a low level, rather than fight it and harm itself. One suggestion links the two ideas: flight's high metabolism leaves damaged molecules and fragments of DNA loose in a bat's cells, which a full-strength alarm would mistake for an infection, so a bat that kept it at full strength would be inflamed after every night's flying.[^damped]

Then comes a check on the reputation itself. In 2020 Nardus Mollentze and Daniel Streicker of the University of Glasgow gathered the known viruses of mammals and birds that also infect people, and asked whether bats carry more of them than other groups do. Bats do carry many, but there are a great many kinds of bats, about one mammal species in five. Once the number of species in each group was allowed for, bats carried about the share their numbers predicted, no more per species than rodents, primates or the other groups.[^count]

**Rabies** is a virus that attacks the nervous system and passes from animal to animal in saliva, usually through a bite. Once symptoms start it is almost always fatal, but a course of vaccine and antibodies given soon after a bite prevents it. In the United States, where dogs are now vaccinated, about seven in ten of the people who catch rabies inside the country catch it from bats. A bat's teeth are so small that a bite can go unnoticed.

blocks.caption: Rabies in bats and people in the United States, in round numbers. The filled dots are bats with rabies.

blocks.text: The numbers are worth holding in proportion. Fewer than 1 in 100 wild bats carries rabies. Of the bats that people send to laboratories for testing, about 5 or 6 in 100 are positive, because those are the bats found on the ground, behaving oddly or in a house, and a sick bat is far more likely to be all three. In Washington State, bats are the only animals known to carry rabies regularly, and a few per cent of the bats sent in for testing each year are positive. The rule follows: most bats are harmless, but a bat you can pick up is more likely to be sick, and its bite can be too small to notice, so never touch one with bare hands. The Bats and people branch of this course covers what to do when one turns up in a house.

blocks.caption: Five questions on long lives
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Which explanation best accounts for bats living several times longer than ground mammals of the same size?
choices: Flying animals are seldom killed by predators, so evolution favours spending energy on bodies that last
Bats hang upside down at rest, which lowers their heart's workload and slows wear
Bats are close relatives of primates, which are long-lived for their size
items.why: If an animal is likely to be eaten soon, a long-lasting body is wasted effort. Bats, which escape most predators by flying, sit well above the lifespan line for their size, and so do birds, the other flyers.

items.ask: A population of mice lives for thousands of generations on an island with no predators. What does the evolutionary theory of ageing predict?
choices: They evolve to age more slowly and live longer than mainland mice
They age at the same rate, since ageing is set by body size alone
They age faster, because without predators they no longer need to stay fit
items.why: With fewer early deaths, a body that lasts pays off. Austad found the same thing in opossums on Sapelo Island, off Georgia.

items.ask: Why can a little brown bat colony take decades to recover from a heavy loss, when mice recover within a year?
choices: Each female raises at most one pup a year, so the colony can grow only about a tenth a year
Bats cannot breed until they are ten years old
Bat pups are too small at birth to survive their first winter
items.why: One pup a year, and only some surviving their first year, means growth of about 10% a year at best. A mouse can raise a litter every month.

items.ask: What did Mollentze and Streicker find when they counted the viruses that infect people in each group of mammals and birds?
choices: Bats carry about as many as expected from how many bat species there are, no more per species than other groups
Bats carry several times more such viruses per species than any other group
Bats carry almost none, and their reputation comes from a few famous cases
items.why: Bats are about one mammal species in five, so they carry many viruses in all. Per species, they were not unusual.

items.ask: About 5 or 6% of bats sent for rabies testing in the United States are positive, but under 1% of wild bats are. Why the difference?
choices: The bats sent in are mostly ones found grounded, sick or indoors, which are more likely to be ill
The laboratories use a more sensitive test than field surveys do
Rabies is more common in bats that live near people
items.why: People send in the bats they find, and a sick bat is the one most likely to be found on the ground or in a house. The tested bats are not a fair sample.

band.title: Banding bats
band.text: Bats are marked with small numbered metal or plastic bands clipped loosely round the forearm, the long bone of the wing, much as birds are ringed on the leg. A band says only when and where the bat was caught first, so a record like this one is a minimum age. A bat in its first summer can be told from an adult by its finger joints, which are still growing and show light gaps when held up to a torch; that is how the banders knew this one was already grown.

austad.title: The opossums of Sapelo
austad.text: Steven Austad compared Virginia opossums on Sapelo Island with mainland ones in South Carolina, published in 1993. The island females lived longer, more of them bred in a second year, and the collagen in their tails, which stiffens with age, aged more slowly.

stored.title: Delayed fertilisation
stored.text: Storing sperm through hibernation lets mating happen in autumn, when bats gather at caves and are fat, and pregnancy start in spring, timed so the pup is born when insects are plentiful. Some tropical bats delay instead the growth of the embryo, after fertilisation.

damped.title: Sensors turned down
damped.text: Among the parts found working weakly in bat cells are a sensor called STING, which detects stray DNA inside a cell, and one called NLRP3, which sets off a strong inflammatory response. Both findings come from studies of bat cells in dishes and a few species, so how far they explain whole bats is still open.

count.title: Allowing for numbers
count.text: Mollentze and Streicker's paper, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2020, compared 415 viruses across groups of mammals and birds. The number of viruses that infect people in each group rose with the number of species in it and with how much those viruses had been studied, and bats lay where their numbers predicted.
